building.name: Oregon Structural Specialty Code (OSSC)
building.edition: 2025 (based on the 2024 International Building Code, with Oregon amendments)
building.local_amendments_note: Portland City Code Title 24 (Building Regulations) adopts the OSSC by reference to the state rule and adds city chapters of its own (administration and permits, flood hazard areas, demolition, clearing and grading, seismic upgrades in Chapter 24.85, and Chapter 32 and parts of Chapter 33 of the International Building Code). The full Title was searched for 'toilet', 'restroom', 'water closet' and 'partition': it holds no rule on toilet counts, toilet partitions or restroom layout. State law (ORS 455.040, state pack) bars a city from setting different requirements on matters the state code covers.

fixtures.basis: Portland adopts the OSSC and OPSC by reference (City Code 24.10.040 and 25.01.020) and Titles 24 and 25, read in full, hold no change to the toilet-count table or its rules. The city's own Building Code Guide 22-10 applies 'OSSC 2902.1' for the required number of plumbing fixtures. The state pack's worked examples stand. Two city interpretations (not amendments) touch the count: (1) Building Official Determination 16-02: in a multi-user all-gender restroom, urinals 'do not count towards the total required number of plumbing fixtures'; (2) Building Code Guide 22-10: for fixture counts in offices, flexible workspaces, conference rooms and breakrooms larger than 750 sf are counted at 1 person per 15 sf, the rest of the office at 1 per 150 sf gross.
fixtures.quote: Similar to the calculation for egress occupant load, PP&D will use a gross OLF of 1:150 for the full square footage within the exterior walls of office buildings, excluding vent shafts and courts. However, for purposes of determining the required number of plumbing fixtures in OSSC 2902.1 and legal building occupancy for seismic retrofit triggers in Portland City Code Chapter 24.85, flexible workspaces, conference rooms, and breakrooms larger than 750 sf will be subtracted from the gross square footage and calculated using an OLF of 1:15. [...] HISTORY: Implemented March 16, 2022.
fixtures.second_quote: RESPONSE 2: Urinals may be provided in multi-user all-gender restrooms, but do not count towards the total required number of plumbing fixtures. [...] RESPONSE 3: The total number of accessible fixtures in a multi-user all-gender restroom shall be determined based on the requirements for water closet compartments in a multi-user facility in 1110.2.4.

permit.note: Neither list names toilet partitions or compartments. The state exemption covers 'nonfixed and movable' partitions up to 5 ft 9 in 'such as cubicle and workspace walls' and 'similar finish work'; toilet partitions are anchored to the floor, wall or ceiling, and whether they fall under either item is not stated. The city's list of work needing a permit names 'Tenant improvements', 'Disabled access upgrades' and 'Move or construct walls, even if non-bearing partitions'. The city's interactive project guide (portland.gov/ppd/commercial-permitting/changing-commercial-space/project-guide) asks whether the project will 'add, remove, or change any fixed structure like a wall, platform, or stage' and tells a user who answers no to every question 'you will not need a permit'; it doesn't mention toilet partitions either.

restrooms_city.rule: Two city rules add to the state's. (1) Portland City Code 23.01.071 (Ordinance 192144, passed February 11, 2026, effective March 13, 2026): single-occupant restrooms in places of public accommodation may not be restricted to a sex or gender identity and must carry signs saying they are for any person; existing single-gender signs must be replaced on or before January 1, 2027; enforcement starts July 1, 2027; no physical changes are required. (2) Building Official Determination 16-02 (September 2016, revised August 2, 2024), the city's reading of the state code for multi-user all-gender restrooms: each toilet enclosed by full-height floor-to-ceiling partitions or walls, door bottom no more than 1 inch above the floor, door top at least 84 inches above the floor, jamb overlapping the door so nothing can be seen from outside, lock with an occupied/vacant indicator, separate ventilation for each toilet enclosure; urinals there must be enclosed the same way and don't count toward the required fixtures.
restrooms_city.quote: 23.01.071 Nondiscrimination Requirements for Single-Occupant Restrooms in Places of Public Accommodation. (Added by Ordinance 192144, effective March 13, 2026.) A. Definitions. 1. Place of public accommodation has the same meaning as defined in ORS 659A.400. 2. Appropriate signage means signage that indicates that single-occupant restrooms are not restricted to a single gender. [...] 3. Single-occupant restroom means a fully enclosed, lockable restroom with one toilet, designed for use by one individual at a time. [...] B. Single-occupant restrooms in places of public accommodation may not be restricted to a specific sex or gender identity and must use appropriate signage to indicate such facilities are designated for use by any person, regardless of sex or gender identity. C. Entities covered by this Chapter 23.01 must comply on or before January 1, 2027, by replacing existing signs on the exterior of single-occupant restrooms restricting use to a single gender with signs indicating that they are for use by all users. Enforcement will commence on July 1, 2027. D. Notwithstanding Section 23.01.080, this Section does not create a private right of action [...]
restrooms_city.second_quote: BOD 16-02: All-Gender Restrooms. [...] QUESTION 1: OSSC Chapter 12 requires each water closet to have a separate compartment with "walls or partitions and a door enclosing the fixtures to ensure privacy." What does this mean for all-gender facilities? RESPONSE 1: Each water closet must be enclosed with full height floor to ceiling partitions or walls. The bottom edge of the door shall be located less than or equal to 1" off the finished floor. The top edge of the door must extend at least 84" above the finished floor but may leave up to a 4" gap above that height. The door jamb must overlap the door in the closed position for the full height of the door to prevent any visual observation from the outside of the partition enclosure. Each water closet must have locking hardware that functions with an indicator showing whether it is occupied or vacant. Each water closet must have separate ventilation. QUESTION 2: Are urinals allowed in all-gender restrooms? RESPONSE 2: Urinals may be provided in multi-user all-gender restrooms, but do not count towards the total required number of plumbing fixtures. Each urinal within multi-user all-gender restrooms must be enclosed in a separate compartment meeting the standards outlined in Question 1 with the exception that a urinal may share a compartment with a single water closet. [...] September 2016 Implementation. Aug 2, 2024 Revised from Code Guide OSSC/29/#1 to building official determination format. Updated to reflect code change and FAQ's.
restrooms_city.third_quote: Ordinance 192144 [...] This ordinance does not mandate the creation of any single-user restrooms or any physical changes to existing restroom facilities. [...] Failure to comply may be reported to Code Review via 311. Portland Permitting and Development will investigate and take further action to enforce this Code for any noncompliant businesses. [...] Passed as amended by Council February 11, 2026
restrooms_city.note: City-owned buildings also follow the city's all-user restroom policy (Resolution 37175 of December 17, 2015, described in the findings of Ordinance 192144; the resolution and Administrative Rule ADM 13.03 were not opened). City Code 23.01.040 C.3 also requires 'reasonable and appropriate accommodations permitting all persons access to restrooms consistent with their expressed gender'.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Portland job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see the Oregon rules Portland enforces.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Portland office buildings, schools, brewpubs and warehouses, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Oregon's building rules set the number of toilets by how many people use the building, and they are the same in every Oregon city. Portland enforces them without changes of its own. The table below shows what that means.
extra_rule_bullets: - **Shared all-gender rooms in Portland:** Portland's building official has set out what the state's privacy rule means in a shared all-gender restroom. Each toilet must be enclosed from floor to ceiling. The door may start no more than 1 inch above the floor and must reach at least 84 inches above it, the frame must overlap the door so nobody can see in, and the lock must show whether the stall is occupied. Each enclosure needs its own ventilation. A urinal in that room needs the same kind of enclosure. Tell us in your quote request if the room is all-gender.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** a one-person restroom must be marked as open to everyone, and its door needs a privacy lock that shows when the room is occupied. A Portland ordinance also covers existing one-person restrooms in places open to the public: signs that limit the room to one gender must be replaced by January 1, 2027, and the city enforces the rule from July 1, 2027. Oregon lets a building meet its toilet count with shared all-gender rooms or with separate men's and women's rooms. Either way, each toilet sits in its own compartment with a door and each urinal has a privacy screen. Oregon law bars discrimination by sex or gender identity in places open to the public and in public schools.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Portland Permitting & Development issues building permits in Portland. Its list of commercial work that needs a permit includes tenant improvements, disabled access upgrades and moving or building walls, non-bearing partitions included. Oregon's building rules exempt finish work such as painting, tiling and cabinets, and movable partitions no taller than 5 feet 9 inches, such as office cubicles. Neither list names toilet partitions. Ask Portland Permitting & Development (503-823-7300) whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.stalls_after: These are minimums, and the men's figures show toilets only, before any are swapped for urinals. An office with 50 people or fewer, or any other space with 30 or fewer, can use a single one-person restroom instead. Where a shared restroom is built for all genders, the count is taken on everyone together rather than half and half, and in Portland urinals in that room don't count toward it.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, Oregon's building rules count an office at one person per 150 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20. For an office's toilet count, Portland counts conference rooms, break rooms and shared work areas larger than 750 square feet at one person per 15 square feet.
page.install_rule: Portland has no city contractor license. Contractors who apply for permits through the city's online system must hold an Oregon Construction Contractors Board license, and Oregon requires that license, with a commercial endorsement, for commercial construction work, specialty trades included. Ask the Construction Contractors Board which endorsement fits the job. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: The contractor needs an Oregon Construction Contractors Board license with a commercial endorsement.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on public projects over $50,000, school district and city buildings included, Oregon law requires at least the wage the state's Bureau of Labor and Industries sets for each trade. For a carpenter on a job in Portland that is $56.69 an hour plus $17.81 in benefits.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** none in Portland. Oregon has no general sales tax or use tax.
page.buyers_extra: - **Brewpubs, taprooms and food halls:** HDPE or phenolic that takes wet floors and heavy evening traffic, with full-height stalls where the room is shared by all genders.

notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether replacing or adding anchored toilet partitions in an existing commercial restroom needs a Portland building permit (Portland Permitting & Development, 503-823-7300, or a free 15-minute appointment). The city's list of work needing a permit names tenant improvements and disabled access upgrades; the state's exempt list names neither toilet partitions nor anything fixed.

Building Official Determination 16-02 was last revised on August 2, 2024, before the 2025 Oregon Structural Specialty Code took effect; it is still on the city's list of determinations. Confirm with Portland Permitting & Development that it stands under the 2025 code, and how it reads the door height ('at least 84 inches above the finished floor but may leave up to a 4 inch gap above that height').

The all-gender bullet matters for quoting: a shared all-gender room in Portland needs full-height, no-sightline enclosures with occupancy-indicator locks, not standard partitions. Check with Abe which product lines meet it before the page promises anything.
The exempt-work list (Section 105.2 of the 2025 Oregon Structural Specialty Code) was read on UpCodes, not on the official ICC-hosted copy.

Carpenter rate: BOLI's page lists its rate books by script, so the current book was found through search. The July 5 and September 3, 2026 books show the same carpenter figures and the October 5, 2026 amendment doesn't touch them. BOLI normally publishes again on January 5: recheck then. The rate is statewide for Carpenter Group 1 with zone pay beyond 30 miles of a reference city's city hall; the current book has no separate regional carpenter rate.
The buyers bullet on brewpubs and the four building types in the lead are editorial, not sourced.

Sales tax: Oregon has none, so the section's heading and closing sentence still mention sales tax; the page says there is none. How Next Partitions itself is taxed on Oregon sales (Corporate Activity Tax, Portland and Multnomah County business taxes) is a question for Abe's accountant.
City-owned buildings follow a separate city all-user restroom policy (Resolution 37175, 2015); it was not opened and is left out of the page.
